prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

More than a hundred dollars of them. It was pure folly. I had to find more glass things to stuff them in. Now a white and purple cloud is breathing in each corner of the room I love. Now a mass of flowers spills down my dining table— each fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the crush. Didn't I watch children shuffle strictly in line, cradle candles that dribbled hot white on their fingers, chanting Latin—just to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Wasn't I sad? Didn't I use to go mucking through streambeds with the skunk cabbage raising bursting violet spears?—Look, the afternoon dies as night begins in the heart of the lilies and smokes up their fluted throats until it fills the room and my lights have to be not switched on. And in close darkness the aroma grows so sweet, so strong, that it could slice me open. It does. I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring and one tall room and the tremble of my phone. I'm not the only one that love makes feel like a dozen flapping bedsheets being ripped to prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in full sun I feel I have been falling headfirst for decades. God, I am so transparent. So light.

Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the exact tone you wish to achieve. 

### Option 1: Lyrical & Literary (Recommended)
*This version elevates the vocabulary and sentence rhythm while preserving the vivid, poetic intensity of the original prose poem.*

> More than a hundred dollars spent—it was sheer folly. I was forced to hunt for additional glass vessels just to hold them. Now, a cloud of white and purple breathes in every corner of the room I cherish. A cascade of flowers spills across my dining table—each bloom fresh-faced, extending delicate leaves into the dense arrangement. 
>
> Did I not watch children march in strict procession, cradling candles that dripped hot white wax onto their fingers as they chanted in Latin—all to fashion Sevilla's Easter? Was I not sorrowful? Did I not once trudge through streambeds where skunk cabbage raised its bursting violet spears? 
>
> Look: the afternoon dies as night takes root in the hearts of the lilies, billowing up their fluted throats until it fills the room, rendering the lights unnecessary. In the intimate darkness, the fragrance grows so sweet, so potent, that it threatens to cut me open—and it does. 
>
> I know I am not the only one whose life is a conditional clause, suspended by the promise of spring, a high-ceilinged room, and the vibration of a phone. I am not the only one whom love transforms into a dozen snapping linens, torn into prayer flags by the gale. Standing in the full glare of the sun, I feel as though I have been falling headlong for decades. Lord, I am so transparent. So light.

---

### Option 2: Elegant Prose (Slightly More Formal)
*This version smoothes out the fragmented thoughts into seamless, sophisticated prose suitable for a memoir or essay.*

> Exceeding a hundred dollars, the purchase was pure folly; I had to search for more glass vases simply to accommodate them all. Now, a breathing cloud of white and purple occupies every corner of the room I love, and a mass of flowers spills over my dining table—each fresh bloom extending delicate leaves into the vibrant cluster. 
>
> Was it not I who watched children march in disciplined lines, cradling candles that dripped hot white wax on their fingers while chanting in Latin to craft Sevilla’s Easter? Was I not filled with sadness? Did I not once wade through streambeds where skunk cabbage thrust its violet spears toward the sky? 
>
> Notice how the afternoon fades as night begins in the core of the lilies, rising like smoke through their fluted throats until it fills the space, leaving no need to turn on the lights. In the close darkness, the scent grows so sweet and powerful it feels capable of cleaving me open—and indeed, it does. 
>
> I know I am not unique in having a life that hangs like a conditional clause upon the essence of spring, a tall room, and the tremor of a phone. Nor am I the only one whom love leaves feeling like bedsheets violently torn into prayer flags by the wind. When I stand in the full heat of the sun, I feel as though I have been falling headfirst for decades. Truly, I am so transparent. So light.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **"Glass things to stuff them in"** $\rightarrow$ Refined to *"glass vessels to hold them"* or *"glass vases simply to accommodate them."*
* **"Mucking through streambeds"** $\rightarrow$ Elevated to *"trudge through"* or *"wade through streambeds."*
* **"Lights have to be not switched on"** $\rightarrow$ Fixed the awkward phrasing to *"rendering the lights unnecessary"* / *"leaving no need to turn on the lights."*
* **"Felt like a dozen flapping bedsheets..."** $\rightarrow$ Enhanced the poetic imagery to *"snapping linens, torn into prayer flags by the gale."*
outputs.L2:
Dropping over a hundred dollars on those blooms was pure madness. I was forced to hunt through the house for extra glass containers just to pack them all in. Now, every corner of my beloved space breathes with a soft haze of white and violet. Across the dining table spills an abundance of fresh flowers, their delicate foliage straining against the crowded arrangement.

Did I not stand by as young children marched in strict procession through Seville, holding candles that dripped hot white wax onto their hands while chanting in Latin for Easter? Was I not steeped in sorrow back then? Didn't I used to trudge through muddy creek beds where purple shoots of skunk cabbage burst from the earth?

Watch how the daylight wanes as shadow creeps out from the center of the lilies, rising like smoke through their narrow throats until darkness saturates the chamber and keeps me from turning on the lamps. In this pitch-black space, their perfume turns so overwhelmingly rich and potent that it feels capable of tearing me open—and indeed, it does.

Surely I am not unique in having my life hinge on the arrival of spring, a room with high ceilings, and the faint vibration of my cell phone. Other people, too, are undone by love—feeling like laundry on a line whipped and torn by gales into sacred flags. When direct sunlight hits me, I feel as though I have spent decades in a downward freefall. My God, I am utterly see-through. Entirely weightless.
outputs.L3:
In a moment of uncharacteristic extravagance, I surrendered to a sudden impulse and purchased an overwhelming abundance of fresh flowers. Bringing them home felt like ushering the vibrant energy of the season directly indoors. As I filled every available vase and jar, the flowers took over, completely transforming my ordinary living space into a lush, breathing sanctuary filled with radiant colors and shifting shadows.

Yet, the blooms carried more than just visual splendor; their appearance unlocked a flood of bittersweet nostalgia. Sitting among them, I was transported back to past springs that had shaped me. The rich, heady scents recalled solemn Easter rituals in Sevilla—the lingering smoke of incense mingling with orange blossoms along narrow, sun-drenched streets during *Semana Santa*. Beneath those urban memories lay even older ones: childhood afternoons lost in nature, wandering barefoot through untamed fields, enveloped by the simple, raw magic of the earth awakening.

As day faded and night fell, the mood in the room subtly shifted. In the stillness of the dark, the lilies began to exhale an intoxicating, almost narcotic fragrance that quickly saturated the air. No longer just a pleasant background note, the overwhelming perfume filled the room to capacity, triggering a profound and almost painfully intense emotional reaction—a sharp, sudden ache of beauty that took my breath away.

In that quiet intensity, I reflected on how deeply human this moment was. It felt less like a private meditation and more like a bridge to a shared human experience. To be alive in the spring is to feel perpetually precarious and expectant, caught in a delicate balance between vulnerability and hope. We are all, at some point, violently upended by the sudden force of love and the unyielding arrival of new beginnings, rendered defenseless by the sheer momentum of life renewing itself.

By the time the night finally yielded to the first pale light of morning, the emotional tempest had cleared, leaving a deep sense of calm in its wake. Surrounded by the quiet blooms, I felt entirely stripped of my usual defenses—weightless, transparent, and completely exposed to the world, yet strangely healed by the revelation.
outputs.L4:
Spring arrived that year not as a gentle awakening, but as a sharp, unbearable exposure. As the earth thawed and the air softened, a quiet ache settled deep within my chest—a restless yearning I could neither name nor ignore. It felt as though winter had kept my grief safely frozen, but the returning light was prying open the seams of my composure. I felt terribly, impossibly visible to the world, raw and unprotected.

Driven by a sudden, irrational impulse to outrun this hollow feeling, I visited the local flower market and bought every lily in sight. It was an act of ridiculous extravagance. I returned home carrying armfuls of long green stems, heavy with unopened alabaster buds. 

Methodically, I set about transforming my living space. I filled every vessel I owned—earthenware crocks, crystal vases, mason jars, and tall water pitchers—with the flowers. I crowded them onto the dining table, lined them up along the windowsill, and placed them on the floor beside my bed. Within hours, my quiet apartment was turned into a dense, indoor sanctuary, a sea of pale green and pristine white.

At first, the silence of the flowers offered a strange comfort. But as the afternoon sun warmed the glass panes, the first buds began to peel back their velvet petals. As they opened, so too did the vault of my memory. 

The sight of the flowers pulled me backward in time, unraveling months of disciplined forgetting. I remembered a past I had tried desperately to bury: the soft cadence of a voice now silent to me, the touch of a hand on my wrist during a long-ago April, and the quiet promise of a love that had promised forever but ended in a sudden, quiet shift. I saw us standing in a garden long since abandoned, framed by the same brilliant light that now poured through my curtains.

As night fell, the lilies bloomed fully, and their fragrance bloomed with them. It was not a subtle perfume, but a thick, narcotic haze that saturated the air. The scent was sweet, heavy, and relentless. Yellow pollen dusted the dark wood of my tables like golden ash. 

I tried to maintain my distance, to sit back and observe them with cool detachment, but the atmosphere was too dense for defenses. The fragrance seemed to seep directly into my lungs, bypassing my mind and striking at the very center of my heart. It washed over my carefully constructed stoicism, dissolving the walls I had built to protect myself from the pain of loss. 

Sitting in the dimming light, enveloped by the intoxicating white blooms, I wept. I wept for the love I had lost, for the time that had passed, and for the sheer, terrifying beauty of being alive to feel it all. 

In that moment of total surrender, the truth of my existence became brilliantly clear. The lilies had not shielded me from my vulnerability; they had forced me to confront it. Love, like spring, is an uncontrollable force of nature. It refuses to let us remain hidden or hardened. Surrounded by the delicate, short-lived blossoms, I realized that to love and to live fully is to accept being rendered glass-thin. Nature does not ask for our permission to undo us; it simply demands that we open, frail and transparent, to the world.
outputs.L5:
For a long time, I lived in the quiet shadow of hesitation. **Didn**’t I have endless days ahead? That was the comforting lie I kept telling myself whenever an opportunity slipped through my fingers. I believed that tomorrow would automatically bring clarity, that circumstances would magically align, and that preparation was something that happened while standing still. But waiting **didn**’t build anything; it only accumulated dust on forgotten dreams.

Everything changed when I realized that the present is the only terrain where action can actually take root. Right **now**, in this precise moment, the path forward opens up. The past is a closed book, and the future is a phantom that vanishes as you approach it, but **now** is where choices are transformed into reality. Excuses lose their weight when confronted with the powerful immediacy of today.

It is no longer enough to settle for mere routine or passive living. I want **more** out of existence—**more** depth, **more** connection, and **more** purpose. Seeking **more** isn't about greed; it is about honoring the dormant potential that sat untouched for far too long. The hesitation of yesterday is gone, replaced by an unwavering commitment to build a meaningful life starting right **now**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about impulse-buying over $100 worth of lilies, focusing on the sensory experience of their scent filling a dark room while waiting anxiously for a phone call.
counterfactuals.output:
It was a hundred and twelve dollars swiped in a fugue state under the harsh fluorescent lights of the midnight bodega—a reckless, towering armful of Casablancas and Stargazers, jammed now into every mason jar, water pitcher, and pint glass I owned. I turned out the lights to hide the mess, but in the pitch-black, the flowers only grew louder. 

The scent does not merely drift; it occupies. It is an airborne velvet, a heavy, narcotic fog of cold wax, crushed cloves, and bruised vanilla pouring from those unseen, flared throats. It thickens the dark until the air feels wet and expensive, filling my lungs with a perfume so sweet it tastes faintly of rot and rust-colored pollen. I am breathing in a flooded greenhouse, drowning in a funeral haze I bought just to feel something happen. 

On the nightstand, the phone rests face-down, a cold slab of black glass. Every phantom pulse in my wrist feels like a vibration; every creak of the floorboards mimics a ringtone that refuses to come. I lie motionless in the gloom, paralyzed by the quiet, while a hundred dollars' worth of cut stems exhale their entire lives all at once around me. The smell coats the back of my throat, rich and suffocating, a golden, perfumed trap set in the dark, waiting for a light to break it—waiting for a voice that is taking forever to call.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a deeply evocative, sensory piece in the style of modern lyric poetry (like Ocean Vuong or Richard Siken). Themes to include: spring, spending too much money on flowers, memories of Easter in Sevilla, skunk cabbage, and the terrifying vulnerability of being in love.
counterfactuals.output:
The clerk swiped my card twice, looking at me 
like I was either crazy or dying, 
and maybe they’re the same thing this time of year. 
Forty-seven dollars for eight stems of french tulips and a bunch of green hellebore 
that will drop their heavy, pale faces onto the kitchen table by Tuesday. 
I am broke. I am disastrously broke, 
but I wanted something in the room that was expensive enough 
to die on purpose. I wanted to show you 
I could afford to waste light.

Outside, the air smells like wet dog and split pine. 
It’s April—that rude, wet thawing. 
Down in the culvert behind the dry cleaner’s, 
the skunk cabbage is doing its ugly, holy work. 
Look at it: pushing up through the black ice, 
generating its own heat, thirty degrees hotter than the frozen mud around it, 
smelling of sulfur and old meat, blooming before anything else 
has the guts to try. 
It cooks itself just to be born. It rots as it opens. 
*Look at me,* it says. *I am making a swamp out of my own fever.*

That’s what I feel like when you put your hand on the back of my neck. 
Like something violently warm stuck in a patch of dirt that hasn’t caught up yet.

I keep thinking of Easter in Sevilla. 2018. 
The midnight procession pressing us against the whitewashed wall 
of Calle Agua. The air thick with *azahar*—that suffocating, sweet rot 
of orange blossoms—mixed with hot beeswax and the iron smell of a million people sweating in the dark. 
Remember the float coming around the corner? 
The Virgen de la Macarena, twelve feet high, swaying under three hundred pounds 
of hammered silver, her face painted with glass tears that caught the flare 
of the brass trumpets. 
The men underneath the wooden frame, hidden by velvet drapery, 
their knees cracking like small dry branches with every step. 
*¡Al cielo con ella!* someone shouted, and they lifted her. 
They lifted all that heavy, terrifying beauty into the night, 
and I turned to you with sugar from a churro still white on my lip, 
and I was so frightened of how much I wanted to kneel down on the cobblestones 
and let the whole procession walk over my ribs.

Devotion is just heatstroke with better music.

Now, in this small apartment, you are cutting the stems at an angle with my butter knife. 
You are so quiet. You have those long, pale fingers 
that look like they were made to hold small birds or unscrew lightbulbs. 
I look at the soft notch between your collarbones and I feel a panic 
so loud it makes my teeth ache. 
You could ruin me with a bad mood. 
You could destroy three years of my life just by walking to the corner store 
and deciding not to come back. 
It’s grotesque, isn't it? How easy we make it for each other. 
How I stand here in my socks, holding a bruised stalk of ranunculus, 
completely unarmored, my chest unzipped and hanging open 
like an old coat on a peg.

The skunk cabbage boils in the ditch. 
The Virgin weeps her small, hard beads of glass into the Andalusian dust. 
And here you are, putting the pink flowers in an old mayonnaise jar, 
setting them in the sunlight. 

*Look,* you say, turning around, your sleeves rolled up to the elbows. 
*Look how bright.*

God help me. 
I don't know how anyone survives a spring like this.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a creative writing passage centered around the phrase: "I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring."
counterfactuals.output:
The radiator clanked its dry, metallic rhythm against the baseboard, a desperate little engine keeping the frost at the windowpane at bay. Outside, the world was dressed in monochrome—slush-brown, overcast-gray, and the dirty white of snow that had survived three rainstorms too many. 

February is a season of suspended sentences. We live entirely in the *if-then*. *If* the sky stops tasting like aluminum, *then* I will finally open the windows. *If* the soil thaws, *then* I will bury the grief I’ve been keeping in the dark back corners of my mind. We walk with our shoulders hitched to our ears, our necks buried in stiff wool, carrying our real, prospective lives in small, sealed envelopes, waiting for the weather to grant us permission to open them.

From my third-floor window, I watched the man across the alley step out onto his fire escape. He was wearing a heavy parka over his pajamas, holding a terracotta pot in his bare hands. It contained nothing but dry, cracked dirt and the pale, brittle skeleton of a geranium from last October. He tapped the side of the pot gently, like a doctor checking for a pulse, then rotated it three inches to catch a thin, heatless stripe of late-afternoon sun. 

He stayed there for a long moment, staring at the dead earth, his breath blooming in small, white clouds before dissolving into the bitter air. 

**I know I'm not the only one whose life is a conditional clause hanging from something to do with spring.**

We are a quiet legion of deferred verbs. The girl at the corner coffee shop who hasn't laughed with her shoulders down since the solstice; the cyclist pedaling through black ice, eyes fixed on a horizon that refuses to yield; myself, holding a pen above a blank notebook, waiting for the temperature to rise five degrees so I can convince myself I am capable of starting over. 

We hang our entire existence on a tilt of the earth. We tell ourselves that who we are in the dark is merely a holding pattern, a rough draft, a breath held in the lungs until the air softens enough to inhale without burning. We stake our happiness on the sudden, reckless audacity of a crocus pushing through frozen turf. 

It is a fragile way to live, dependent entirely on the mercy of the calendar. But as I watched the man on the fire escape step back inside, leaving his pot of dead soil perfectly aligned with that fragile beam of light, I realized it wasn't foolishness at all. 

It was patience. It was the slow, stubborn grammar of survival, waiting for the universe to finally complete the sentence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a dramatic first-person monologue about someone who bought way too many flowers to cope with longing, blending vivid nature imagery with modern elements like a vibrating phone?
counterfactuals.output:
There is no floor left. 

I bought out the corner bodega first. Then the florist on 4th. By noon, I was standing in the wholesale greenhouse on the edge of the city, my hands shaking as I piled armfuls of crushed, bleeding ranunculus into the back of a taxi. 

Look at this place. It’s an absurdity. It’s a terrarium for a lunatic. 

Hydrangeas the size of human heads are suffocating the bookshelf. Delphiniums—toxic, impossible blue—spike up toward the ceiling fan like lightning caught in slow motion. I have eucalyptus hanging over the doorframes like wet green lace, and the air is so thick with the heavy, narcotic grease of gardenias that I can barely draw a clean breath. My fingers are stained yellow with pollen. I have crushed stems beneath my bare heels until my kitchen floor slicked over with sap and bruised leaves. 

I thought… God, I don’t know what I thought. I thought if I filled the void with enough living things, I wouldn’t hear the echo of you walking out. I thought if I made the silence smell like jasmine and damp earth, it wouldn't feel like a grave. I wanted to build a forest so dense, so wild, that even your memory couldn't find its way out.

Instead, it’s just dying. All of it. A room full of cut stems, drowning in stale water, slowly starving on hardwood floors. 

And then—

*(A low, sharp rumble vibrations cut through the room.)*

Somewhere beneath that hill of bruised pink peonies on the glass coffee table, my phone lights up. 

*Bzz. Bzz.*

The cold, mechanical pulse vibrates straight through the glass, shaking a shower of dead petals onto the floorboards. A square of violent blue light cuts through the dark velvet of the blossoms. 

*Bzz.*

It’s a tiny, digital twitch in a suffocating jungle. A modern, glowing nerve ending poking out of a rotting meadow. 

My heart hits my ribs like a trapped bird. Is that your name flickering under the leaves? Is it your voice, trying to reach me through forty pounds of dying flora? Or is it just a reminder for a life I’ve completely abandoned, a ghost in a machine calling out to a ghost in a garden?

I stand here, knee-deep in water and broken stems, smelling of sap and desperation, watching the flowers dance every time the phone hums. 

I don't know if I should dig for it. I don't know if I can bear to pull back the petals and find out it isn’t you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of prose that connects the following images: a dining table overwhelmed with purple and white flowers, children chanting in Latin carrying dripping candles, bedsheets tearing in the wind like prayer flags, and feeling weightless in full sun.
counterfactuals.output:
The polished mahogany of the dining table had ceased to exist beneath a tide of purple and white. Vases overflowed with bruised lilacs, milk-pale hydrangeas, and wild nightshade, their heavy, sweet decay blooming so thick in the humid air that breathing felt like swallowing velvet. It was a funeral for the season, or perhaps a feast for something uninvited.

Through the darkened doorway came the procession. Barefoot and solemn, the children moved in a slow, hypnotic sway, their voices rising in a cool, ancient Latin—a rhythmic chant of *requiem* and *lumen* that echoed against the high plaster ceilings. In their small, tallow-stained hands, they carried tall wax tapers. Hot grease dripped over their knuckles like melting bone, splashing onto the floorboards with soft, rhythmic hissings. 

They did not stop at the table, but passed through the French doors into the blinding light outside, where a sudden summer gale had whipped up from the valley. 

On the long clotheslines stretching across the yard, white bedsheets snapped and frayed in the violent draft, tearing in the wind like prayer flags stranded on some sacred, storm-swept peak. Shreds of linen ripped free, soaring into the sky like pale birds. 

I stepped out behind the children, leaving the suffocating perfume of the bruised flowers behind. The heat of the candles dissolved into the immense, blinding brightness above. As the wind caught the torn fabric and the Latin chant drifted away into the sky, the ground beneath my feet simply ceased to matter. The anchor of my body gave way, leaving me floating, suspended, and entirely weightless in the full, unblinking sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
